A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLIP-based, facial-component-guided Deepfake detector. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and supplementary materials support comparison despite extensive rewriting and reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original cross-dataset detection results, component ablations, data-efficiency experiments, perturbation tests and diffusion-image evaluations.

after.justification: v3 reports original detection experiments and ablations, including WildDeepfake results and an evaluation of collected HeyGen avatar videos.

M1.justification: The principal architecture, FCG objective and spatial-only diffusion adaptation are retained. However, v2 Section 3.2 specifies the temporal residual block W as two fully connected layers with ReLU, whereas v3 Section 3.3 calls it a residual linear layer. The PDFs do not resolve whether this reflects a component change or abbreviated documentation.

E1.justification: v3 adds WildDeepfake across the cross-dataset evaluations and introduces 56 videos from 28 creators using HeyGen avatars. These substantially extend coverage to internet-sourced Deepfakes and a contemporary avatar-generation scenario. The existing video benchmarks and four diffusion-generator evaluations are retained.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds CADDM, Yan et al., Choi et al., Hong et al. and LAA-Net. Table 4 adds full fine-tuning and shallow/deep VPT comparisons; linear probing, renamed LCP, and EVL already appeared in v2. Conversely, the FF++ robustness comparison drops Xception, Face X-ray, LipForensics, FTCN and TALL-Swin, retaining RealForensics.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported learning rate from 1e-3 to 1e-4 and weight decay from 1e-4 to 1e-3. The stated DFDC evaluation subset changes from 3,215 to 3,814 videos, and the ViT-B/16 evaluation configuration disappears. These are reported setting revisions, without establishing that experiments were rerun. The batch descriptions remain equivalent: 240 total versus 60 per GPU across four GPUs.

E4.justification: v3 removes v2's temporal-attribute combination sweep, explicit missing-face/large-motion analysis, and extensive-versus-simple augmentation comparison. Its attention analysis adds a fully fine-tuned CLIP comparator and individual-clip visualizations. Component, facial-part, data-efficiency and perturbation analyses remain, with revised evidence; the diffusion robustness evaluation is retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's averaging of attention maps over 100 clips does not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced: Table 1 reports CDF AUROC of 92.3 in v2 versus 95.0 in v3, and DFDC 81.2 versus 81.8. Revised training settings and DFDC sampling prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains. Diffusion zero-shot average AP changes from 92.2 in v2 Table 7 to 81.0 in v3 Table 9. Ablation, LOO, data-fraction and robustness scores also change, alongside new WildDeepfake and avatar results.

T1.justification: The FCG and classification-loss equations and ViT attribute-extraction algorithm retain their mathematical substance. Superscript notation and tensor-shape exposition are revised, but neither version introduces additional theorems, proofs or formal theoretical guarantees.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the spatial/temporal side-network decoder, FCG and cross-dataset generalization. v3 removes the abstract's specific 0.9-point average and 4.4-point DFDC improvement claims, and explicitly promotes parameter efficiency and robustness alongside data efficiency as headline benefits.

C2.justification: The facial-component interpretation changes materially: v2 Section 6.6 identifies skin as critical, whereas v3 Section 8.1 identifies eyes as most important and describes all exclusions as causing slight declines. v3 also adds the limitation that sparse frame sampling can miss high-frequency artifacts, and explicitly acknowledges weaker FF++ robustness than RealForensics while retaining the cross-dataset robustness argument.

D1.justification: v3 adds inference timing of 1.5 seconds per three-second video on an A5000 GPU and describes VPT prompt placement. Reported training cost changes from 14 to approximately 16 GPU hours. Conversely, v2's half-precision disclosure, landmark-based tracking stabilization, missing-face handling instructions and detailed diffusion-data sample counts are omitted.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands research positioning through recent work on identity leakage, style latent flows, latent-space augmentation, multi-label ranking and LAA-Net. It also explicitly acknowledges Ojha et al.'s CLIP-based generic synthetic-image detection, sharpening the distinction between that prior work and adaptation for facial Deepfake detection.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Spatial and temporal subsections exchange order, some analyses move between the main text and supplement, and limitations and other closing sections are added. The title, author list and mathematical terminology also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, adds an introductory comparison graphic and individual attention visualizations, and redraws the framework and temporal-module diagrams. Tables gain dataset and comparator-information columns and are reorganized; v2's separate FF++ and CDF robustness tables become v3 Table 6. These changes extend beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: Broader evaluations, stronger adaptation comparisons, revised figures and explicit limitations strengthen v3, but diagnostic analyses and reproducibility details are lost. Reporting also becomes inconsistent: v2 Tables 7 and 9 agree on 92.2 zero-shot clean AP, whereas v3 Tables 9 and 10 report 81.0 and 100. Its claimed CDF lead is insufficiently qualified given Table 1's 95.0 for Ours and published 95.4 for LAA-Net. These unresolved tradeoffs prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
